blocks.text: This chapter deals with two major areas of physics, namely the polarization of transverse waves and gravitational waves. Physical optics, with reference to polarization, deals with the behaviour of light waves and their interaction with matter.

Interference and diffraction effects prove the wave nature of light. These phenomena, however, do not tell us whether the light waves are longitudinal or transverse. Polarization of light suggests that the light waves are transverse in character.

In transverse mechanical waves, such as those produced in a stretched string, the vibrations of the particles of the medium are perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the waves. The vibrations can be oriented along the vertical, the horizontal or any other direction (Fig. 8.1). In each of these cases the transverse mechanical wave is said to be polarized.

blocks.alt: Two strings, each held at its lower left end by a hand and running diagonally up to the right. On the upper string (a) the wave goes up and down, with a vertical double arrow beside it; on the lower string (b) the wave goes side to side in a horizontal plane, with a horizontal double arrow beside it.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.1: Transverse waves on a string polarized (a) in a vertical plane, and (b) in a horizontal plane (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.1).

blocks.title: Plane of polarization
blocks.text: The plane of polarization is the plane containing the direction of vibration of the particles of the medium and the direction of propagation of the wave.

A light wave produced by an oscillating charge consists of a periodic variation of the electric field vector E accompanied by the magnetic field vector B, at right angles to each other. Ordinary light has components of vibration in all possible planes; such light is unpolarized. On the other hand, if the vibrations are confined to only one plane, the light is said to be polarized. Unpolarized light is shown in Fig. 8.2: light from an incandescent bulb has vibrations in all directions. Examples of unpolarized light sources are sunlight, incandescent light bulbs, fluorescent light bulbs, and light from a candle or fire.

blocks.alt: A glowing incandescent bulb at the bottom left. A line from the bulb leads up to a burst of yellow arrows pointing outward in all directions round one point.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.2: An unpolarized light, due to incandescent bulb, has vibrations in all directions (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.2).

blocks.title: Polarization
blocks.text: Polarization is the process by which the electric and magnetic vibrations of light waves are restricted to a single plane of vibration. It is a property exhibited by transverse waves only, such as light waves; it does not occur for longitudinal waves such as sound waves. The orientation of the electric field vector E of light waves in a specific direction is the basis of polarization.
How can unpolarized light be polarized?

items: Passing the light through a polarizing filter (for example a polaroid sheet).
Employing certain optical crystals or materials (for example calcite or quartz).

blocks.text: The most common method by which unpolarized light can be polarized is by passing it through a polarizing filter, such as a polarizing beam splitter or a polaroid sheet. When unpolarized light passes through the filter, only the electric field vector which is parallel to the axis of the filter can pass through it, while all other vectors are blocked; the resultant light then becomes polarized (Fig. 8.3). Thus, in simple words, the process of transforming unpolarized light into polarized light is called polarization.

blocks.alt: A ray (blue line) travels down to the right. Before the filter, red E arrows point in many directions. The ray passes through a polarized filter with vertical lines and a vertical axis arrow. After the filter there is only one vertical red E arrow.
